source: The engineering advances associated with deep learning (e.g. Paszke et al., 2019; Abadi et al., 2015) provide powerful tools for modeling brain information processing for complex, naturalistic tasks (LeCun et al., 2015).

source: How to leverage the new big data to evaluate the new big models, however, is an open problem (Stevenson and Kording, 2011; Sejnowski et al., 2014; Smith and Nichols, 2018; Kriegeskorte and Douglas, 2018).

claim: Representational geometry is an important concept for understanding neural population codes.
source: An important concept for understanding neural population codes is the concept of representational geometry (Shepard and Chipman, 1970; Edelman et al., 1998; Edelman, 1998; Norman et al., 2006; Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008a; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008b; Connolly et al., 2012; Xue et al., 2010; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Yamins et al., 2014; Cichy et al., 2014; Haxby et al., 2014; Freeman et al., 2018; Kietzmann et al., 2019; Stringer et al., 2019; Chung et al., 2018; Chung and Abbott, 2021; Kriegeskorte and Wei, 2021).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to foundational and recent work.

claim: Neural activity patterns can be viewed as points in the multivariate neural population response space of a brain region.
source: Neural activity patterns that represent particular pieces of mental content, such as the stimuli presented in a neurophysiological experiment, can be viewed as points in the multivariate neural population response space of a brain region.
evidence: This is a conceptual framework statement supported by the representational geometry literature.

claim: The representational geometry is characterized by the matrix of distances among the points.
source: The representational geometry is the geometry of these points. The geometry is characterized by the matrix of distances among the points.
evidence: Definition of representational geometry.

claim: The distance matrix abstracts from the roles of individual neurons and provides a summary characterization of the neural population code.
source: This distance matrix abstracts from the roles of individual neurons and provides a summary characterization of the neural population code that can be directly compared among animals and between brain and model representations (e.g. a cortical area and a layer of a neural network model).
evidence: Describes the utility of the distance matrix approach.

claim: The representational geometry provides a multivariate characterization of a neural population code that can be motivated as a generalization of linear decoding analyses.
source: The representational geometry provides a multivariate characterization of a neural population code that can be motivated as a generalization of linear decoding analyses.
evidence: Conceptual relationship between representational geometry and decoding.

claim: A linear decoder reveals a single projection of the geometry.
source: A linear decoder reveals a single projection of the geometry.
evidence: Describes the relationship between linear decoding and representational geometry.

claim: The full distance matrix captures what information is available in any linear projection when measured after a transform that renders the noise isotropic.
source: The full distance matrix (when measured after a transform that renders the noise isotropic) captures what information is available in any linear projection (Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen, 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Representational similarity analysis (RSA) is a popular method for analyzing representational geometries.
source: A popular method for analyzing representational geometries (Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013) on which we build here is representational similarity analysis (RSA; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008a; Nili et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational RSA papers.

claim: RSA is a three-step process.
source: RSA is a three-step process (Figure 1): In the first step, RSA characterizes the representational geometry of the brain region of interest (ROI) by estimating the representational distance for each pair of experimental conditions (e.g. different stimuli). The distance estimates are assembled in a representational dissimilarity matrix (RDM). We use the more general term 'dissimilarity' here to include dissimilarity measures that are not distances or metrics in the mathematical sense, such as crossvalidated distance estimators that can return negative values. This relaxation enables inclusion of measures that are not biased by the noise in the data (Kriegeskorte et al., 2007; Nili et al., 2014; Walther et al., 2016; Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen, 2019a), returning values distributed symmetrically about 0, when the true distance is 0, but patterns are noisy estimates. In the second step, each model is evaluated by the accuracy of its prediction of the data RDM. To this end, an RDM is computed for each model representation. Each model's prediction of the data RDM is evaluated using an RDM comparator, such as a correlation coefficient. In the third step, models are inferentially compared to each other in terms of their RDM prediction accuracy to guide computational theory.
evidence: Description of RSA methodology with reference to Figure 1 and supporting citations.

claim: RSA is widely used and has gained additional popularity with the rise of image-computable representational models like deep neural networks.
source: RSA is widely used (Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013; Haxby et al., 2014; Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen, 2019a) and has gained additional popularity with the rise of image-computable representational models like deep neural networks (e.g. Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Yamins et al., 2014; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Mehrer et al., 2017; Kriegeskorte, 2015; Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016; Xu and Vaziri-Pashkam, 2021; Konkle and Alvarez, 2022; Cichy et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations showing widespread use and application to deep neural networks.

claim: There has been important recent progress with methods for estimating representational distances and measures of RDM prediction accuracy.
source: There has been important recent progress with methods for estimating representational distances (step 1) as well as measures of RDM prediction accuracy (step 2). For RDM estimation, biased and unbiased distance estimators with improved reliability have been proposed (Nili et al., 2014; Cai et al., 2019; Walther et al., 2016). For quantification of the RDM prediction accuracy, the sampling distribution of distance estimators has been derived and measures of RDM prediction accuracy that take the dependencies between dissimilarity estimates into account have been proposed (Diedrichsen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent methodological advances.

claim: Existing statistical inference methods for RSA have important limitations.
source: However, existing statistical inference methods for RSA (step 3) have important limitations. Established RSA inference methods (Nili et al., 2014) provide a noise ceiling and enable comparisons of fixed models with generalization to new subjects and conditions. However, they cannot handle flexible models, can be severely suboptimal in terms of statistical power, and have not been thoroughly validated using simulated or real data where ground truth is known.
evidence: Identifies limitations of existing methods, motivating the current work.

claim: Model-comparative inference with generalization to new conditions is not trivial because new conditions extend an RDM and the evaluation depends on pairwise dissimilarities, thus violating independence assumptions.
source: Model-comparative inference with generalization to new conditions is not trivial because new conditions extend an RDM and the evaluation depends on pairwise dissimilarities, thus violating independence assumptions.
evidence: Describes a methodological challenge addressed by the paper.

claim: Standard methods for statistical inference do not handle multiple random factors — subjects and conditions in RSA.
source: Standard methods for statistical inference do not handle multiple random factors — subjects and conditions in RSA.
evidence: Identifies a limitation of standard statistical methods.

claim: Flexible models are essential for RSA.
source: Flexible models, that is models that have parameters enabling them to predict different RDMs, are essential for RSA (Diedrichsen et al., 2018; Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on flexible models in RSA.

claim: Evaluation of flexible models requires methods that are unaffected by overfitting to either subjects or conditions to avoid a bias in favor of more flexible models.
source: Evaluation of such models requires methods that are unaffected by overfitting to either subjects or conditions to avoid a bias in favor of more flexible models.
evidence: Describes a methodological requirement for evaluating flexible models.

claim: The paper introduces novel bootstrapping methods that support generalization of model-comparative statistical inferences to new subjects, new conditions, or both simultaneously.
source: We introduce novel bootstrapping methods that support generalization of model-comparative statistical inferences to new subjects, new conditions, or both simultaneously, as required to support the theoretical claims researchers wish to make.
evidence: Describes the main methodological contribution.

claim: The paper introduces a novel crossvalidation method for estimation of the RDM prediction accuracy of flexible models.
source: We also introduce a novel crossvalidation method for estimation of the RDM prediction accuracy of flexible models, that is models with parameters fitted to the data (Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen, 2016).
evidence: Describes a methodological contribution with supporting citations.

claim: Theories do not always make a specific prediction for the representational geometry due to unknown parameters.
source: This is important, because theories do not always make a specific prediction for the representational geometry. There may be unknown parameters, such as the relative prevalences of different tuning functions (Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Jozwik et al., 2016) in the neural population or properties of the measurement process (Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen, 2016).
evidence: Motivates the need for flexible models with supporting citations.

claim: The combination of 2-factor bootstrap and 2-factor crossvalidation methods enables statistical comparisons among fixed and flexible models that generalize across subjects and conditions.
source: The combination of our 2-factor bootstrap and 2-factor crossvalidation methods enables statistical comparisons among fixed and flexible models that generalize across subjects and conditions.
evidence: Describes the capability of the combined methodology.

claim: The new inference methods were thoroughly validated using simulations and neural activity data.
source: We thoroughly validate the new inference methods using simulations and neural activity data.
evidence: Describes the validation approach, with results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Extensive simulations based on deep neural network models enable testing of model-comparative inference in a setting where the ground-truth model is known.
source: Extensive simulations based on deep neural network models and models of the measurement process enable us to test model-comparative inference in a setting where the ground-truth model (the one that actually generated the data) is known.
evidence: Describes the simulation-based validation approach.

claim: The simulations confirm the validity of the inference procedures and their ability to generalize to the populations of subjects and/or conditions.
source: These simulations confirm the validity of the inference procedures and their ability to generalize to the populations of subjects and/or conditions.
evidence: Summary of simulation results.

claim: The methods were validated on real data from calcium imaging (mouse) and functional MRI (human).
source: We also validated the methods on real data from calcium imaging (mouse) and functional MRI (human).
evidence: Describes validation using real neural data.

claim: For both calcium imaging and fMRI datasets, conclusions generalize from an experimental dataset to the entire dataset.
source: For both datasets, we confirm that conclusions generalize from an experimental dataset (a subset of the real data) to the entire dataset (which serves as a stand-in for the population).
evidence: Summary of validation results on real data.

claim: The statistical inference methodology is available in a new open-source RSA toolbox written in Python.
source: The statistical inference methodology described in this paper is available in a new open-source RSA toolbox written in Python (https://github.com/rsagroup/rsatoolbox, copy archived at Schütt, 2023).
evidence: Direct statement about software availability with URL.

claim: The paper introduces a new representational dissimilarity estimator for electrophysiological recordings based on the KL-divergence between Poisson distributions.
source: This paper also introduces a new representational dissimilarity estimator for electrophysiological recordings of patterns of firing rates across a population of neurons, based on the KL-divergence between Poisson distributions (Appendix 2)
evidence: Describes a methodological contribution with reference to Appendix 2.

claim: The proposed inferential methods work for any representational dissimilarity measure and any RDM comparator.
source: The proposed inferential methods work for any representational dissimilarity measure and any RDM comparator.
evidence: Describes the generality of the methods.

claim: Inference using only subject variability does not justify generalization to different experimental conditions.
source: However, inference then only takes the variability over subjects into account and thus does not justify generalization to different experimental conditions (e.g. different stimuli).
evidence: Identifies a limitation of the simple approach.

claim: Computational neuroscience usually pursues insights that generalize not only to a population of subjects but also to a population of conditions.
source: Computational neuroscience usually pursues insights that generalize not only to a population of subjects but also to a population of conditions (Yarkoni, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation discussing generalization in neuroscience.

claim: To support generalization to the population of conditions statistically, uncertainty estimates must treat the experimental conditions as a random sample from a population.
source: To support generalization to the population of conditions statistically, we require uncertainty estimates that treat the experimental conditions as a random sample from a population (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008a), whether or not the subjects are treated as a random sample.
evidence: Describes a statistical requirement with supporting citation.

claim: Bootstrap methods estimate the variance of experimental outcomes by sampling from the measured data with replacement.
source: Bootstrap methods estimate the variance of experimental outcomes by sampling from the measured data with replacement, treating the measured data as an approximation to the population (Efron and Tibshirani, 1994).
evidence: Describes bootstrap methodology with citation to foundational text.

claim: When bootstrapping conditions, entries corresponding to the dissimilarity of any condition with itself are excluded from comparisons between RDMs.
source: When we bootstrap-resample conditions, we obtain RDMs of the same size as the original RDMs, but some of the conditions will be repeated. Here, we exclude the entries that correspond to the dissimilarity of any condition with itself from the comparisons between RDMs.
evidence: Describes a specific methodological choice.

claim: Simulations confirm that the bootstrap procedure for conditions yields a good estimate of variability when sampling new conditions with the same subjects.
source: Simulations confirm that this procedure yields a good estimate of how variable the results are when we sample new conditions with the same subjects (Figures 4a and 6g).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in figures.

claim: A naive 2-factor bootstrap approach triple-counts the variance contributed by the measurement noise.
source: However, our simulations and theory here show that a naive 2-factor bootstrap approach triple-counts the variance contributed by the measurement noise (Methods, Estimating the uncertainty of our model-performance estimates, Figures 4c and 7c).
evidence: Supported by theoretical analysis and simulation results.

claim: The naive 2-factor bootstrap is not unique to RSA; it will triple-count variance related to measurement noise for any experiment with two factors jointly determining the experimental outcome.
source: This effect is not unique to RSA; a naive 2-factor bootstrap will triple-count variance related to the measurement noise for any type of experiment in which two factors (here subject and condition) jointly determine the experimental outcome.
evidence: Generalization of the finding beyond RSA.

claim: The naive 2-factor bootstrap estimate contains the noise variance component three times instead of once.
source: Thus, the original bootstrap estimate contains the noise variance component three times instead of once
evidence: Result of theoretical analysis.

claim: The overestimate of the variance renders the naive 2-factor bootstrap conservative and not optimally powerful.
source: The overestimate of the variance renders the naive 2-factor bootstrap conservative and not optimally powerful.
evidence: Consequence of the triple-counting problem.

claim: Multiple simulations show that the corrected estimate approximates the correct variance better than the uncorrected 2-factor bootstrap.
source: We show in multiple simulations that this estimate approximates the correct variance better than the uncorrected 2-factor bootstrap (Figures 4c and 7c).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in figures.

claim: The variance estimate is bounded from above and below to stabilize the estimator and eliminate the possibility of a negative variance estimate.
source: To stabilize the estimator and eliminate the possibility of a negative variance estimate, we bound the estimate from above and below.
evidence: Describes a methodological choice for practical implementation.

claim: Bounding slightly biases the variance estimate but reduces its variability and ensures that it is strictly positive.
source: Bounding slightly biases the variance estimate, but reduces its variability and ensures that it is strictly positive.
evidence: Describes the trade-off of the bounding procedure.

claim: Flexible models have parameters to be fitted to the brain-activity data.
source: We often want to test flexible models, that is models that have parameters to be fitted to the brain-activity data.
evidence: Definition of flexible models.

claim: Feature weighting is required when a model is not meant to specify a priori how prevalent different tuning profiles are in the neural population.
source: Feature weighting is required when a model is not meant to specify a priori how prevalent different tuning profiles are in the neural population or in the measured signals. For example, for deep neural network representations to match brain responses well, it is usually necessary to weight the features (e.g. Yamins et al., 2014; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Khaligh-Razavi et al., 2017; Storrs et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to work using feature weighting.

claim: A flexible measurement model may be necessary to account for the process of measurement, which may subsample, average, or distort neural responses.
source: A flexible measurement model may be necessary to account for the process of measurement, which may subsample, average, or distort neural responses.
evidence: Describes the need for flexible measurement models.

claim: fMRI voxels average the neural activity locally, which can be modeled with a parameter for the local averaging range.
source: For example, fMRI voxels average the neural activity locally, which can be modeled with a parameter for the local averaging range
evidence: Example of measurement model flexibility.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings may preferentially sample certain classes of neurons.
source: and electrophysiological recordings may preferentially sample certain classes of neurons (Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen, 2016).
evidence: Example of measurement bias with supporting citation.

claim: Crossvalidation is used to avoid the bias in model-performance estimates that can result from overfitting of flexible models.
source: To avoid the bias in the model-performance estimates that can result from overfitting of flexible models, we use crossvalidation.
evidence: Describes the use of crossvalidation.

claim: Crossvalidation means partitioning the dataset into separate test sets, fitting models to all but one set, and evaluating on the held-out set.
source: Crossvalidation means that we partition the dataset into separate test sets. In each fold of crossvalidation, we then fit the models to all but one set and evaluate on the held-out set.
evidence: Definition of crossvalidation procedure.

claim: Taking the average over the folds yields a single performance estimate.
source: Taking the average over the folds yields a single performance estimate.
evidence: Standard crossvalidation procedure.

claim: Crossvalidation is performed over both conditions and subjects to avoid overestimating the generalization performance of flexible models.
source: As for bootstrapping, crossvalidation is performed over both conditions and subjects so as to avoid overestimating the generalization performance of flexible models when tested on new subjects and new conditions drawn from the populations of subjects and conditions sampled in the actual experiment (Figure 1b).
evidence: Describes the 2-factor crossvalidation approach with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: The smallest possible number of conditions to perform crossvalidation is 6, which would yield three test conditions for twofold crossvalidation.
source: Because the RDM for the test set must contain multiple values to allow a sensible comparison, the smallest possible number of conditions to perform crossvalidation is 6, which would yield three test conditions for twofold crossvalidation.
evidence: Practical constraint on crossvalidation.

claim: For small numbers of conditions, twofolds are used; threefolds for ≥12 conditions, fourfolds for ≥24 conditions, and fivefolds for ≥40 conditions.
source: For small numbers of conditions, we use twofolds. We use threefolds for ≥12 conditions, fourfolds for ≥24 conditions, and fivefolds for ≥40 conditions.
evidence: Practical guidelines for choosing number of folds.

claim: To estimate uncertainty about crossvalidated model performances, the same bootstrap methods as for fixed models are used.
source: To estimate our uncertainty about the crossvalidated model performances, we use the same bootstrap methods as for fixed models. To do so, we need to perform crossvalidation on each bootstrap sample. We call this procedure bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation.
evidence: Describes the bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation procedure.

claim: Different ways to partition the data into test sets lead to different overall evaluations of the models in crossvalidation.
source: In any crossvalidation, different ways to partition the data into test sets lead to different overall evaluations of the models.
evidence: Describes a property of crossvalidation.

claim: When partitioning conditions into disjoint test sets in RSA, the effect of different partitionings is particularly strong because dissimilarities between conditions in separate test sets do not contribute to the evaluation in any fold.
source: When we partition the conditions set into disjoint test sets in RSA, this effect is particularly strong, because dissimilarities between conditions in separate test sets do not contribute to the evaluation in any fold.
evidence: Describes a specific challenge for RSA crossvalidation.

claim: The variance in evaluations created by random assignment would vanish if exhaustive crossvalidation with all possible partitionings were performed.
source: The variance in the evaluations created by this random assignment is generated by our analysis and would vanish if we performed repeated cycles of crossvalidation with all possible partitionings of the conditions set into test sets.
evidence: Theoretical property of exhaustive crossvalidation.

claim: Exhaustive crossvalidation is usually prohibitively expensive in terms of computation time, especially in bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation.
source: Unfortunately, such exhaustive crossvalidation will usually be prohibitively expensive in terms of computation time, especially in bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation.
evidence: Practical limitation of exhaustive crossvalidation.

claim: An estimate of the variance for exhaustive crossvalidation can be directly computed from two or more crossvalidation cycles using random partitionings for each bootstrap sample.
source: Thus, we can directly compute an estimate of the variance we expect for exhaustive crossvalidation from two or more crossvalidation cycles using random partitionings for each bootstrap sample.
evidence: Describes the correction formula for crossvalidation variance.

claim: The reliability of the bootstrap estimate of the variance improves more when increasing the number of bootstrap samples than when increasing the number of crossvalidation cycles per bootstrap sample.
source: Our simulations show that the reliability of the bootstrap estimate of the variance of the model-performance estimate improves more when we increase the number of bootstrap samples than when we increase the number of crossvalidation cycles per bootstrap sample (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Using only two crossvalidation cycles per bootstrap sample is recommended.
source: Thus, we recommend using only two crossvalidation cycles per bootstrap sample.
evidence: Recommendation based on simulation results.

claim: The crossvalidation approach provides model-performance estimates that are not biased by overfitting of flexible models to either subjects or conditions.
source: This crossvalidation approach provides model-performance estimates that are not biased by overfitting of flexible models to either subjects or conditions.
evidence: Summary of the crossvalidation approach's properties.

claim: Fixed and flexible models with different numbers of parameters can be robustly compared with generalization over conditions and/or subjects.
source: Fixed and flexible models with different numbers of parameters can be robustly compared with generalization over conditions and/or subjects.
evidence: Describes the capability of the method.

claim: The method can handle any model that can be fitted efficiently enough.
source: The method can handle any model that can be fitted efficiently enough (for the types of flexible models we actually implemented, see Methods, Flexible models).
evidence: Describes the generality and limitation of the method.

claim: The statistical tests for model comparison are valid, controlling the false-positive rate at the nominal level.
source: First, we establish that the statistical tests for model comparison are valid, controlling the false-positive rate at the nominal level.
evidence: Summary of validation results.

claim: A matrix-normal model is used to simulate the null scenario for model comparison where two models that predict distinct RDMs are exactly equal in their RDM prediction accuracy.
source: This requires simulating data under the null hypothesis, where two models that predict distinct RDMs are exactly equal in their RDM prediction accuracy. We use a matrix-normal model to simulate this null scenario for model comparison.
evidence: Describes the simulation approach for validation.

claim: The estimates of uncertainty about model performance correctly capture the true variability for different generalization schemes in more realistic simulated scenarios based on neural network models.
source: Second, we show that the estimates of our uncertainty about model performance correctly capture the true variability for different generalization schemes in more realistic simulated scenarios based on neural network models.
evidence: Summary of validation results.

claim: The bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation scheme correctly accounts for the overfitting of flexible models.
source: Third, we validate the inference procedure for flexible models, confirming that our bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation scheme correctly accounts for the overfitting of flexible models.
evidence: Summary of validation results for flexible models.

claim: A frequentist test is valid when the rate of false positives does not exceed the specified error rate α.
source: A frequentist test is valid when the rate of false positives (i.e. the rate of positive results when the null hypothesis is true) does not exceed the specified error rate α (e.g. 5%).
evidence: Definition of test validity.

claim: The validity of model-comparative inference is checked where the null hypothesis is that two models perform equally well at explaining the representational geometry.
source: Here, we check the validity of model-comparative inference, where the null hypothesis is that the two models perform equally well at explaining the representational geometry.
evidence: Describes the specific null hypothesis tested.

claim: Scenarios are simulated where two models predict distinct geometries but perform equally well on average at predicting the true representational geometry.
source: We simulate scenarios where two models predict distinct geometries, but perform equally well on average at predicting the true representational geometry.
evidence: Describes the simulation design for validation.

claim: Condition-response matrices are generated by sampling from matrix-normal density models.
source: To simulate situations where two different models perform equally well, we generated condition-response matrices (containing an activity level for each combination of condition and response channel) by sampling from matrix-normal density models.
evidence: Describes the data generation method.

claim: For matrix-normal data, the covariance across conditions captures the similarity among condition-related response patterns and determines the expected squared Euclidean-distance RDM.
source: For matrix-normal data, the covariance across conditions captures the similarity among condition-related response patterns and determines the expected squared Euclidean-distance RDM (Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017).
evidence: Theoretical property of matrix-normal distributions with supporting citation.

claim: All model-comparative subject-only bootstrap tests were found to be valid.
source: We first evaluated the bootstrap in the scenario, where the goal is to generalize across subjects only. All model-comparative subject-only bootstrap tests were found to be valid (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Validation result with reference to figure.

claim: Inflated false-positive rates were observed for subject-only bootstrap tests only when using a small sample of subjects (<20).
source: Inflated false-positive rates were observed for subject-only bootstrap tests only when using a small sample of subjects (<20).
evidence: Validation result identifying a limitation.

claim: Bootstrapping for generalization to new conditions was conservative, showing false-positive rates substantially below 5%.
source: Next, we tested bootstrapping for generalization to new conditions. In this scenario, the bootstrap methods were all conservative, showing false-positive rates substantially below 5% (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Validation result with reference to figure.

claim: The conservative result for condition bootstrapping is expected because no random selection of conditions was included in the data simulation.
source: This is expected, because we did not include any random selection of conditions in our data simulation, but enforced the H0 exactly for the measured conditions.
evidence: Explanation of the conservative result.
