source: In these simulations, all techniques that only take subjects into account as a random factor fail catastrophically (Appendix 1—figure 1), with false-positive rates growing with the number of simulated subjects and reaching 60% at 40 simulated subjects.
evidence: Validation result showing the importance of accounting for condition sampling.

claim: Bootstrap tests that include condition sampling all remain valid, with false-positive rates below the nominal 5%.
source: In contrast, our bootstrap tests that include condition sampling all remain valid, including the uncorrected 2-factor bootstrap and our new corrected 2-factor bootstrap with false-positive rates below the nominal 5%.
evidence: Validation result showing the validity of the proposed methods.

claim: The uncorrected 2-factor bootstrap was extremely conservative.
source: However, the uncorrected 2-factor bootstrap was extremely conservative.
evidence: Validation result showing a limitation of the uncorrected method.

claim: The tests are valid in simple simulated H0 scenarios where the false-positive rate can be estimated.
source: We conclude that the tests are valid in these simple simulated H0 scenarios, where we are able to estimate the false-positive rate.
evidence: Summary of validation results.

claim: In more realistic simulations using neural network models and real data, it is not possible to simulate distinct models that predict the data RDM equally well.
source: In more realistic simulations using neural network models and real data, we can no longer simulate distinct models that predict the data RDM equally well.
evidence: Limitation of the more realistic simulations.

claim: Ideally, the bootstrap-estimated variance should match the true variance such that the RU is 1.
source: Ideally, we would like the bootstrap-estimated variance to match the true variance such that the RU is 1.
evidence: Criterion for evaluating bootstrap accuracy.

claim: Model discriminability is defined as a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) where the signal is the magnitude of model-performance differences and the noise is the nuisance variation.
source: To measure how sensitive our analysis is to differences in model performance (e.g. comparing layers of a deep neural network), we define the model discriminability as a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The signal is the magnitude of model-performance differences, which is measured as the variance across models of their average of performance estimates across simulations. The noise is the nuisance variation, which includes subject and condition sample variation along with measurement noise. The noise is measured as the average across models of the variance of performance estimates across simulations.
evidence: Definition of the SNR metric.

claim: A higher SNR indicates greater sensitivity to differences in model performance.
source: A higher SNR indicates greater sensitivity to differences in model performance: differences between models are larger relative to the variation of model-performance estimates over repeated simulations.
evidence: Interpretation of the SNR metric.

claim: The SNR measure does not depend on the accuracy of the bootstrap because bootstrap estimates of variances do not enter this statistic.
source: Note that this measure does not depend on the accuracy of the bootstrap because the bootstrap estimates of the variances do not enter this statistic.
evidence: Property of the SNR metric.

claim: Simulated true voxel responses were generated as local averages of the activities of close-by units in the feature maps of AlexNet layers.
source: We simulated true voxel responses as local averages of the activities of close-by units in the feature maps of layers of the model.
evidence: Description of the simulation procedure.

claim: The response of each simulated voxel was a local average of unit responses, weighted according to a 2D Gaussian kernel over locations and a vector of nonnegative random weights across features.
source: The response of each simulated voxel was a local average of unit responses, weighted according to a 2D Gaussian kernel over the locations of the feature map multiplied by a vector of nonnegative random weights (drawn uniformly from the unit interval) across the features.
evidence: Description of the simulation procedure.

claim: Hemodynamic-response timecourses were simulated and measurement noise was added.
source: We then simulated hemodynamic-response timecourses and added measurement noise.
evidence: Description of the simulation procedure.

claim: The covariance structure of the noise was determined by the overlap of the simulated voxels' averaging regions over space and a first-order autoregressive model over time.
source: The covariance structure of the noise was determined by the overlap of the simulated voxels' averaging regions over space and a first-order autoregressive model over time.
evidence: Description of the noise model in the simulation.

claim: The simulated data were subjected to a standard general linear model (GLM) analysis to estimate the condition-response matrix.
source: The simulated data were subjected to a standard general linear model (GLM) analysis to estimate the condition-response matrix.
evidence: Description of the analysis procedure.

claim: Variation over conditions was generated by using randomly sampled natural images from ecoset as input to the AlexNet model.
source: Variation over conditions was generated by using randomly sampled natural images from ecoset (Mehrer et al., 2017) as input to the AlexNet model.
evidence: Description of how condition variability was simulated.

claim: Variation over subjects was generated by randomly choosing a new location and a new vector of feature weights for each voxel of a new simulated subject.
source: Variation over subjects was generated by randomly choosing a new location and a new vector of feature weights for each voxel of a new simulated subject.
evidence: Description of how subject variability was simulated.

claim: The aim of the analyses was to infer which layer of AlexNet the simulation was based on.
source: The aim of the analyses was always to infer which layer of AlexNet the simulation was based on.
evidence: Description of the analysis goal, also shown in Figure 3.

claim: The rate of erroneously finding an alternative model outperforming the true data-generating model was very low (1.524% at 5% uncorrected significance level) when the type of bootstrap matches the simulated level of generalization.
source: As expected, the rate of erroneously finding an alternative model outperforming the true data-generating model was very low (not shown) whenever the type of bootstrap matches the simulated level of generalization because the true layer has a higher average performance than the other models. At the 5% uncorrected significance level, the proportion of cases where any other layer performed significantly better than the true (data-generating) layer was only 1.524%.
evidence: Validation result showing low error rates.

claim: Tests against the best other layer significantly favor this other layer in only 0.694% of cases.
source: Tests against the best other layer (chosen based on all data) significantly favor this other layer in only 0.694% of cases.
evidence: Validation result showing very low error rates for the most stringent comparison.

claim: Multiple-comparison correction would reduce model-selection error rates even further.
source: Multiple-comparison correction would reduce these model-selection error rates even further.
evidence: Inference about the effect of multiple-comparison correction.

claim: When simulating condition sampling, the true variance across conditions is accurately estimated for 40 or more conditions.
source: To test generalization to either new conditions or new subjects (but not both simultaneously), we kept the other dimension constant. When simulating condition sampling, the true variance across conditions is accurately estimated for 40 or more conditions (Figure 4a)
evidence: Validation result with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: The true variance across conditions is overestimated by 1-factor bootstrap resampling when there are less than about 40 conditions, rendering the inference conservative.
source: and is overestimated by 1-factor bootstrap resampling of conditions (rendering the inference conservative) when we have less than about 40 conditions (Figure 4a).
evidence: Validation result with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: When simulating subject sampling, the true variance across subjects is accurately estimated for 20 or more subjects.
source: When simulating subject sampling, the true variance across subjects is accurately estimated for 20 or more subjects (Figure 4b)
evidence: Validation result with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: The true variance across subjects is underestimated by 1-factor bootstrap resampling when there are very few subjects, invalidating the inference.
source: and is underestimated by 1-factor bootstrap resampling of subjects (invalidating the inference) when we have very few subjects (Figure 4b).
evidence: Validation result with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: The corrected 2-factor bootstrap estimates the overall variation caused by random sampling of subjects and conditions and by measurement noise much more accurately than the naive 2-factor bootstrap.
source: To test our corrected 2-factor bootstrap method's ability to generalize to new subjects and new conditions simultaneously, we simulated sampling of both conditions (stimuli) and subjects in our simulations. The corrected 2-factor bootstrap estimates the overall variation caused by random sampling of subjects and conditions and by measurement noise much more accurately than the naive 2-factor bootstrap (Figure 4c).
evidence: Validation result with reference to Figure 4c.

claim: Cases where an incorrect model significantly outperformed the true model occurred in only 0.3% of simulations with the corrected 2-factor bootstrap, even without multiple-comparison correction.
source: Cases where an incorrect model (not the data-generating model) significantly outperformed the true model occurred in only 0.3% of simulations with the corrected 2-factor bootstrap, even without any multiple-comparison correction.
evidence: Validation result showing very low error rates.

claim: The corrected 2-factor bootstrap method yields accurate estimates of the variance when the dataset is large enough (≥20 subjects, ≥40 conditions) and the type of bootstrap matches the population sampling simulated.
source: Overall, we found that the new more powerful corrected 2-factor bootstrap method yields accurate estimates of the variance across the simulated populations of subjects and conditions when the dataset is large enough (≥20 subjects, ≥40 conditions) and the type of bootstrap matches the population sampling simulated (subject, condition, or both).
evidence: Summary of validation results.

claim: Model discriminability (SNR) increases monotonically with the number of measurements, affording greater power for model-comparative inference.
source: The model discriminability (SNR) increases monotonically with the number of measurements, affording greater power for model-comparative inference.
evidence: Result from simulations.

claim: Model discriminability increases with the amount of data according to a power law.
source: Model discriminability increases with the amount of data according to a power law (straight line in log–log plot; Figure 4d–f).
evidence: Result from simulations with reference to figures.

claim: Increasing the number of measurements helps most for the factor that causes most variability of the performance estimates.
source: In general, increasing the number of measurements helps most for the factor that causes most variability of the performance estimates, rendering generalization harder.
evidence: General principle derived from simulation results.

claim: In the deep-neural-network-based simulations, the variability over subjects is smaller than the variability across conditions.
source: For example, in our deep-neural-network-based simulations, the variability over subjects is smaller than the variability across conditions (Figure 4g).
evidence: Result from simulations with reference to Figure 4g.

claim: In the simulation, it increases statistical power more to collect data for more conditions than more subjects.
source: In this simulation, it thus increases statistical power more to collect data for more conditions.
evidence: Inference from simulation results.

claim: An intermediate voxel size yielded the highest model-performance discriminability as measured by the SNR.
source: An intermediate voxel size (Gaussian kernel width) yielded the highest model-performance discriminability as measured by the SNR (Figure 4h, see Appendix 5 for more discussion on this topic).
evidence: Result from simulations with reference to Figure 4h.

claim: The simulated ground truth set the spatial weights for each voxel to a Gaussian with a standard deviation of 5% of the image size and randomly weighted the feature maps.
source: As the simulated ground truth, we set the spatial weights for each voxel to a Gaussian with a standard deviation of 5% of the image size (full width at half maximum FWHM ≈ 11.77%) and randomly weighted the feature maps (with weights drawn independently for each voxel and feature map uniformly at random from the unit interval; details in Methods, Neural-network-based simulation).
evidence: Description of the simulation setup.

claim: Models were generated without knowing the ground truth of how voxels average local features.
source: We then used models that a researcher could generate without knowing the ground truth of how voxels average local features.
evidence: Description of the model generation approach.

claim: Feature maps were smoothed with Gaussians of different sizes to capture voxel averaging across retinotopic locations.
source: To capture voxel averaging across retinotopic locations, we smoothed the feature maps with Gaussians of different sizes.
evidence: Description of the modeling approach.

claim: Three methods were used to deal with averaging across feature maps: computing RDMs after averaging across feature maps, computing the expected RDM for the weight sampling, or computing RDMs without feature-map averaging.
source: To capture voxel averaging across feature maps, we (1) generated RDMs computed after taking the average across feature maps at each location (avg), (2) computed the expected RDM for the weight sampling implemented in the simulation (weighted), or (3) computed RDMs without any feature-map averaging (full).
evidence: Description of the modeling approaches.

claim: Two types of flexible model were defined: selection models and nonnegative linear-combination models.
source: We combined these building blocks into two types of flexible model: selection models and nonnegative linear-combination models.
evidence: Description of the flexible model types.

claim: In a selection model, fitting is implemented as selection of the best among a finite set of RDMs.
source: In a selection model, fitting is implemented as selection of the best among a finite set of RDMs.
evidence: Definition of selection models.

claim: In linear-combination models, fitting consists in finding nonnegative weights for a set of basis RDMs to maximize RDM prediction accuracy.
source: In linear-combination models, fitting consists in finding nonnegative weights for a set of basis RDMs, so as to maximize RDM prediction accuracy.
evidence: Definition of linear-combination models.

claim: The bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation yielded accurate estimates of the uncertainty, with relative uncertainties close to 1.
source: We found that our bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation (corrected 2-factor bootstrap with adjustment for excess crossvaldation variance) yielded accurate estimates of the uncertainty. The relative uncertainties were close to 1 (Figure 5b).
evidence: Validation result with reference to Figure 5b.

claim: The model-performance discriminability (SNR) was primarily determined by how accurately the different models were able to recreate the true measurement model.
source: The model-performance discriminability (SNR) was primarily determined by how accurately the different models were able to recreate the true measurement model (Figure 5c).
evidence: Result from simulations with reference to Figure 5c.

claim: The highest SNRs were achieved when the assumed model matched exactly.
source: The highest SNRs were achieved when the assumed model matched exactly (weighted feature treatment and voxel size 0.05), but the model variants which allowed for some fitting still yield high SNRs.
evidence: Result from simulations.

claim: Analyses that take the averaging across space and features into account yielded the highest average model performance for the true model.
source: Analyses that take the averaging across space and features into account yielded the highest average model performance for the true model.
evidence: Result from simulations.

claim: Analyses that ignore averaging over space or features lead to lower SNRs and systematically selected the wrong layer.
source: In contrast, analyses that ignore averaging over space or features (the full feature set selection model and some of the fixed models) not only lead to lower SNRs (as seen in Figure 5c), but also systematically selected the wrong layer, because a higher average performance was achieved by a different layer than the one we used for generating the data (not shown).
evidence: Result from simulations showing the importance of proper measurement models.

claim: When the true voxel sampling is unknown, flexible models are needed to account for voxel sampling to recover the underlying data-generating computational model.
source: We conclude that when the true voxel sampling is unknown, flexible models are needed to account for voxel sampling, so as to enable us recover the underlying data-generating computational model with our model-comparative inference.
evidence: Conclusion from simulation results.

claim: Fixed models based on incorrect assumptions about voxel sampling can lead to low model-performance discriminability and incorrect inferences about which model is the true model.
source: Fixed models based on incorrect assumptions about the voxel sampling can lead to low model-performance discriminability (SNR) and even to incorrect inferences as to which model is the true model.
evidence: Conclusion from simulation results.

claim: Real human fMRI data from a large openly available experiment where humans viewed pictures from ImageNet was used for validation.
source: To test our methods under realistic conditions, we used real human fMRI (this section) and mouse calcium-imaging data (next section). We resampled data from a large openly available fMRI experiment in which humans viewed pictures from ImageNet (Horikawa and Kamitani, 2017).
evidence: Description of the validation data with citation.

claim: Real data contain various noise sources, individual differences, signal shapes, and distributions that are difficult to simulate accurately without using measured data.
source: These data contain various noise sources, individual differences, signal shapes, and distributions that are difficult to simulate accurately without using measured data.
evidence: Motivation for using real data for validation.

claim: A data-based simulation was implemented to create realistic synthetic data whose ground-truth RDM is known.
source: We therefore implemented a data-based simulation to create realistic synthetic data, whose ground-truth RDM we knew (Figure 6).
evidence: Description of the validation approach with reference to Figure 6.

claim: The entire dataset was used as a stand-in for the population a researcher might wish to generalize to.
source: We used the entire dataset as a stand-in for the population a researcher might wish to generalize to.
evidence: Description of the validation approach.

claim: For each cortical area, the mean RDM using all data served as a ground-truth RDM for datasets sampled from that area and as a model RDM for datasets sampled from all areas.
source: For each cortical area, we computed the mean RDM using all data (all runs and subjects). Each area's mean RDM served as a ground-truth RDM for datasets sampled from that area and as a model RDM for datasets sampled from all areas.
evidence: Description of how ground-truth and model RDMs were defined.

claim: The model comparison aimed to recover which cortical area a dataset was subsampled from.
source: The model comparison we attempted aims to recover which cortical area a dataset was subsampled from.
evidence: Description of the validation goal.

claim: The simulation enables checking whether uncertainty estimates are correct for model-performance estimates based on real data.
source: The simulation enables us to check whether our uncertainty estimates are correct for model-performance estimates based on real data.
evidence: Purpose of the fMRI-based simulation.

claim: The strength of noise, the number of runs, and the number of conditions were varied in the fMRI simulation.
source: We varied the strength of noise, the number of runs, and the number of conditions (i.e. viewed images).
evidence: Description of simulation parameters.

claim: The number of subjects was not varied because the original dataset contains only five subjects, which precludes informative resampling of subjects.
source: We did not vary the number of subjects because the original dataset contains only five subjects, which precludes informative resampling of subjects.
evidence: Explanation of a limitation in the simulation design.

claim: New voxel timecourses were created for each sampled run while preserving the spatial structure and serial autocorrelation of the noise.
source: To increase the variability of the resampled datasets beyond sampling from the 35 measurement runs and to vary the noise strength, we created new voxel timecourses for each sampled run while preserving the spatial structure and serial autocorrelation of the noise.
evidence: Description of the noise simulation procedure.

claim: Results from the fMRI simulation were largely similar to those of the neural-network-based simulations.
source: Results were largely similar to those of the neural-network-based simulations (Figure 6f, g).
evidence: Summary of validation results with reference to figures.

claim: For the RU, there is a convergence toward the expected ratio (1), validating the bootstrap procedure for real fMRI data.
source: For the RU, which measures the accuracy of our bootstrap variance estimates, we see a convergence toward the expected ratio (dashed line at 1), validating the bootstrap procedure for real fMRI data.
evidence: Validation result for fMRI data.

claim: For the model-performance discriminability (SNR), the same power-law increase with the number of conditions and runs was found as in neural-network-based simulations.
source: For the model-performance discriminability (SNR), we find the same power-law increase with the number of conditions and the number of runs used as data.
evidence: Validation result for fMRI data.

claim: The regions are discriminable on the basis of their RDMs estimated from fMRI given five subjects' data when a sufficient number of stimuli (≥30) and runs (≥16) is used.
source: These results suggest that the regions are discriminable on the basis of their RDMs estimated from fMRI given five subjects' data when a sufficient number of stimuli (≥30) and runs (≥16) is used.
evidence: Conclusion from fMRI simulation results.

claim: A large calcium-imaging dataset of responses of mouse visual cortex to natural images was used for validation.
source: We can also adjudicate among models of the representational geometry on the basis of direct neural measurements, such as electrophysiological recordings or calcium-imaging data. These measurement modalities have very different statistical properties than fMRI. To test our methods for this kind of data, we performed a resampling simulation based on a large calcium-imaging dataset of responses of mouse visual cortex to natural images (de Vries et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of the validation data with citation.

claim: The calcium-imaging dataset contains recordings from six visual cortical areas: V1, LM, PM, RL, AM, and AL.
source: This dataset contains recordings from six visual cortical areas: primary visual cortex (V1), laterointermediate (LM), posteromedial (PM), rostrolateral (RL), anteromedial (AM), and anterolateral (AL) visual area (Figure 7a).
evidence: Description of the data with reference to Figure 7a.

claim: The overall mean RDM for each area was used as a ground-truth model and the data were subsampled to create simulated datasets.
source: As in the previous section, we used the overall mean RDM for each area as a ground-truth model and subsampled the data to create simulated datasets for which we know the ground-truth RDM.
evidence: Description of the validation approach.

claim: Different numbers of stimulus repetitions, neurons, mice, and stimuli were used to vary the amount of information afforded by each simulated dataset.
source: We used different numbers of stimulus repetitions, neurons, mice, and stimuli to vary the amount of information afforded by each simulated dataset.
evidence: Description of simulation parameters.

claim: The crossnobis estimator of representational dissimilarity was used for all calcium-imaging analyses.
source: We used the crossnobis estimator of representational dissimilarity for all analyses here.
evidence: Description of the analysis method.

claim: Cortical areas vary in the reliability of the estimated RDMs but can be discriminated reliably when using all data.
source: We analyzed the overall discriminability of the brain areas (Figure 7b). Although cortical areas vary in the reliability of the estimated RDMs, they can be discriminated reliably when using all data.
evidence: Result from calcium-imaging data analysis with reference to Figure 7b.

claim: Correct variance estimates were observed for the corrected 2-factor bootstrap in the calcium-imaging simulation.
source: We used the RU to assess whether our bootstrap variance estimates are correct for these data (Figure 7c). We resampled all factors (subjects, stimuli, runs, and cells) to generate simulted datasets. Correspondingly, the analysis used bootstrapping over both subjects and stimuli. We observed correct variance estimates for the corrected 2-factor bootstrap.
evidence: Validation result with reference to Figure 7c.

claim: The uncorrected 2-factor bootstrap was conservative, substantially overestimating the true variance in the calcium-imaging simulation.
source: The uncorrected 2-factor bootstrap was conservative, substantially overestimating the true variance.
evidence: Validation result comparing corrected and uncorrected methods.

claim: More subjects, more stimuli, more runs, and more cells all increased the SNR in the calcium-imaging simulation.
source: To understand how the model-comparative power depends on experimental parameters and analysis choices, we analyzed the model-discriminability SNR. We found that more subjects, more stimuli, more runs, and more cells all increased the SNR just as in our fMRI and neural-network-based simulations (Figure 7d).
evidence: Result from calcium-imaging simulation with reference to Figure 7d.

claim: Taking the noise covariance into account for computing the crossnobis RDMs improves the SNR.
source: Furthermore, we find that taking the noise covariance into account for computing the crossnobis RDMs in the first-level analysis improves the SNR (Figure 7e).
evidence: Result from calcium-imaging simulation with reference to Figure 7e.

claim: Univariate noise normalization is better than no noise normalization.
source: Univariate noise normalization (implemented by using a diagonal noise covariance matrix) is better than no noise normalization.
evidence: Result from calcium-imaging simulation.

claim: Multivariate noise normalization is slightly better than univariate noise normalization.
source: Multivariate noise normalization is slightly better than univariate noise normalization (Walther et al., 2016).
evidence: Result from calcium-imaging simulation with supporting citation.

claim: Different RDM comparators yield the best model discriminability for different cortical areas.
source: In addition, we find that different RDM comparators yield the best model discriminability for different cortical areas (Figure 7g).
evidence: Result from calcium-imaging simulation with reference to Figure 7g.

claim: Whitened RDM comparators are better on average, but there are cases where unwhitened RDM comparators perform slightly better.
source: The whitened RDM comparators are better on average, but there are cases where the unwhitened RDM comparators perform slightly better.
evidence: Result from calcium-imaging simulation.

claim: Which RDM comparator affords the best power for model comparison depends on the concrete experiment.
source: Thus, it remains dependent on the concrete experiment (with a particular choice of conditions, tested models and underlying representational geometry), which RDM comparator affords the best power for model comparison (Diedrichsen et al., 2020).
evidence: Conclusion from results with supporting citation.

claim: The inference procedures enable generalization to new measurements, new subjects, and new conditions.
source: We present new methods for inferential evaluation and comparison of models that predict brain representational geometries. The inference procedures enable generalization to new measurements, new subjects, and new conditions, treat flexible models correctly using crossvalidation, and work for any representational dissimilarity estimator and RDM comparator.
evidence: Summary of the methods' capabilities.

claim: The inference methods treat flexible models correctly using crossvalidation.
source: The inference procedures enable generalization to new measurements, new subjects, and new conditions, treat flexible models correctly using crossvalidation, and work for any representational dissimilarity estimator and RDM comparator.
evidence: Summary of the methods' capabilities.

claim: The inference methods work for any representational dissimilarity estimator and RDM comparator.
source: The inference procedures enable generalization to new measurements, new subjects, and new conditions, treat flexible models correctly using crossvalidation, and work for any representational dissimilarity estimator and RDM comparator.
evidence: Summary of the methods' generality.

claim: For fixed and flexible models, the inference methods support all combinations of generalization: to new measurements, to new subjects, to new conditions, and to both new subjects and new conditions simultaneously.
source: For fixed as well as flexible models, our inference methods support all combinations of generalization: to new measurements using the same subjects and conditions, to new subjects, to new conditions, and to both new subjects and new conditions simultaneously.
evidence: Summary of the methods' capabilities.

claim: The methods were validated using simulated data as well as calcium-imaging and fMRI data, showing that the inferences are correct.
source: We validated the methods using simulated data as well as calcium-imaging and fMRI data, showing that the inferences are correct.
evidence: Summary of validation results.

claim: Inferential statistics is about generalization from experimental random samples to the underlying populations.
source: Inferential statistics is about generalization from the experimental random samples to the underlying populations.
evidence: Definition of inferential statistics.

claim: The level of generalization must be carefully considered at the stage of designing experiments and analyses and at the stage of interpreting results.
source: We must carefully consider the level of generalization, both at the stage of designing our experiments and analyses and at the stage of interpreting the results.
evidence: Methodological recommendation.

claim: The lowest level of inferential generalization is to new measurements, where conclusions are expected to hold only for replications of the experiment in the same animals using the same conditions.
source: The lowest level of inferential generalization is to new measurements. Our conclusions in this scenario are expected to hold only for replications of the experiment in the same animals using the same conditions.
evidence: Definition of the lowest level of generalization.

claim: Inferential generalization to new subjects may not be possible in case studies or when the number of animals is insufficient.
source: Inferential generalization to new subjects may not be possible, for example, in case studies or when the number of animals (e.g. two macaques) is insufficient.
evidence: Describes limitations on generalization to subjects.

claim: Generalization to new conditions is not needed when all conditions relevant to the claims have been sampled.
source: Generalization to new conditions is not needed when all conditions relevant to our claims have been sampled. For example, Ejaz et al., 2015 studied the representational similarity of finger movements in primary motor cortex. All five fingers were sampled in the experiments and there are no other fingers to generalize to.
evidence: Example where condition generalization is not needed with citation.

claim: If generalization to the population of subjects is desired, a sufficiently large sample of subjects is needed.
source: If generalization to the population of subjects is desired, we need a sufficiently large sample of subjects.
evidence: Requirement for subject generalization.

claim: The subject-based t-test method is valid, controlling false-positive rates at their nominal values in matrix-normal simulations.
source: We showed that this method is valid, controlling false-positive rates at their nominal values in our matrix-normal simulations (Methods, Frequentist tests for model evaluation and model comparison).
evidence: Validation result.

claim: The variance across subjects is a good estimate of the variance across the population of subjects.
source: The variance across subjects here is a good estimate of the variance across the population of subjects.
evidence: Statistical property.

claim: The interpretation of results using only subject variance must be restricted to the exact set of experimental conditions used in the experiment.
source: However, the interpretation of the results must be restricted to the exact set of experimental conditions used in the experiment.
evidence: Limitation of subject-only generalization.

claim: Inferences are often meant to generalize to a population of conditions.
source: We often would like our inferences to generalize to a population of conditions.
evidence: Common goal in neuroscience research.

claim: When evaluating computational models of vision, researchers are interested in models that dominate for a population of visual stimuli, not just the particular stimuli presented.
source: For example, when evaluating computational models of vision, we are not usually interested in determining which models dominate just for the particular visual stimuli presented in our experiment. We are interested in models that dominate for a population of visual stimuli.
evidence: Example of the need for condition generalization.

claim: Model-comparative inference can generalize to the population of conditions that the experimental conditions were randomly sampled from.
source: Model-comparative inference can generalize to the population of conditions that the experimental conditions were randomly sampled from.
evidence: Capability of the proposed methods.

claim: The inference requires bootstrapping because RDM prediction accuracy cannot be assessed for single conditions.
source: The inference requires bootstrapping, because RDM prediction accuracy cannot be assessed for single conditions.
evidence: Justification for using bootstrapping.

claim: If generalization simultaneously across conditions and subjects is desired, the corrected 2-factor bootstrap approach provides accurate estimates of uncertainty about model performances.
source: If we want to generalize simultaneously across conditions and subjects, then the corrected 2-factor bootstrap approach provides accurate estimates of our uncertainty about model performances.
evidence: Summary of the corrected 2-factor bootstrap capability.

claim: The uncertainty estimates from the corrected 2-factor bootstrap support valid inferential model comparisons, comparisons to the lower bound of the noise ceiling, and tests against chance performance.
source: These uncertainty estimates support valid inferential model comparisons, comparisons to the lower bound of the noise ceiling, and tests against chance performance.
evidence: Summary of the types of inference supported.

claim: Results are expected to generalize to new subjects and conditions drawn from the respective populations sampled randomly in the experiment.
source: We expect the results to generalize to new subjects and conditions drawn from the respective populations sampled randomly in the experiment.
evidence: Interpretation of results from the corrected 2-factor bootstrap.

claim: Performance estimates for flexible models must not be biased by overfitting to measurement noise, subjects, or conditions.
source: Our performance estimates for flexible models must not be biased by overfitting to measurement noise, subjects, or conditions.
evidence: Requirement for evaluating flexible models.

claim: A novel 2-factor crossvalidation scheme enables evaluation of models' predictive accuracy when simultaneously generalizing to new subjects and/or new conditions.
source: To avoid this bias, we use a novel 2-factor crossvalidation scheme that enables us to evaluate models' predictive accuracy when simultaneously generalizing to new subjects and/or new conditions.
evidence: Description of the methodological contribution.

claim: The 2-factor crossvalidation is nested in the 2-factor bootstrap procedure for estimating uncertainty.
source: The 2-factor crossvalidation is nested in our 2-factor bootstrap procedure for estimating uncertainty.
evidence: Description of how the methods are combined.

claim: Using two crossvalidation cycles with different data partitionings for each bootstrap sample enables accurate removal of the excess variance introduced by crossvalidation.
source: By using two crossvalidation cycles with different data partitionings for each bootstrap sample, we can accurately remove the excess variance introduced by crossvalidation.
evidence: Description of the variance correction procedure.

claim: The methods are fully general in that inference can be performed on any model for which the user provides a fitting and an RDM prediction method.
source: Our methods are fully general in that inference can be performed on any model for which the user provides a fitting and an RDM prediction method.
evidence: Description of the generality of the methods.

claim: The complexity of the models is limited by the requirement that each model needs to be fitted thousands of times in the bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation scheme.
source: In practice, the complexity of the models is limited by the requirement that we need to fit each model thousands of times in our bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation scheme. Thus, we need a sufficiently fast and reliable fitting method for the model.
evidence: Practical limitation of the methods.

claim: If fitting the model many times is not feasible or if the data RDMs do not provide sufficient constraints, one solution is to fit all models using a separate set of neural data before the inferential analyses.
source: If fitting the model so often is not feasible or if the data RDMs do not provide sufficient constraints, one solution is to fit all models using a separate set of neural data before the inferential analyses.
evidence: Alternative approach for complex models.

claim: When models are fitted on separate neural data, all conclusions are conditional on the fitting data: Inference will generalize to new test data assuming models are fitted on the same fitting data.
source: This approach is appropriate when many parameters are to be fitted, as is the case in nonlinear systems identification approaches as well as linear encoding models (Wu et al., 2006), where a large set of neural fitting data is required. All conclusions are then conditional on the fitting data: Inference will generalize to new test data assuming models are fitted on the same fitting data.
evidence: Limitation of the alternative approach with supporting citation.

claim: The proposed methods support fitting of lower-parametric models as part of the model-comparative inference, obviating the need for separate neural data for fitting when applicable.
source: Our methods support fitting of lower-parametric models as part of the model-comparative inference. When applicable, this approach obviates the need for separate neural data for fitting and supports stronger generalization (not conditional on the neural fitting data).
evidence: Advantage of the proposed methods.

claim: The methods enable comparison of a model's RDM prediction performance against other models, against the noise ceiling, and against chance performance.
source: Our methods enable comparison of a model's RDM prediction performance (1) against other models, (2) against the noise ceiling, and (3) against chance performance.
evidence: Summary of supported tests.

claim: The first two tests (against other models and against the noise ceiling) are central to the evaluation of models.
source: The first two of these tests are central to the evaluation of models.
evidence: Evaluation of the importance of different tests.

claim: The test against chance performance is often reported but represents a low bar that most models should be expected to pass.
source: The test against chance performance is often also reported, but represents a low bar that we should expect most models to pass.
evidence: Evaluation of the test against chance.

claim: RDM correlations tend to be positive even for very different representations because physically highly similar stimuli tend to be similar in all representations.
source: In practice, RDM correlations tend to be positive even for very different representations, because physically highly similar stimuli or conditions tend to be similar in all representations.
evidence: Observation about RDM correlations.

claim: A significant Pearson correlation indicates a dependency but does not demonstrate that the dependency is linear.
source: Just like a significant Pearson correlation indicates a dependency, but does not demonstrate that the dependency is linear, a significant RDM prediction result indicates the presence of stimulus information, but does not lend strong support to the particular model.
evidence: Analogy explaining the interpretation of RDM correlations.

claim: Significant prediction performance per se should not be interpreted as evidence for a particular model (the single-model-significance fallacy).
source: We should resist interpreting significant prediction performance per se as evidence for a particular model (the single-model-significance fallacy; Kriegeskorte and Douglas, 2019b).
evidence: Methodological warning with supporting citation.

claim: Theoretical progress requires that each model be compared to alternative models and to the noise ceiling.
source: Theoretical progress instead requires that each model be compared to alternative models and to the noise ceiling.
evidence: Recommendation for rigorous model evaluation.

claim: The interpretation of chance performance, where the RDM comparator equals 0, depends on the chosen RDM comparator.
source: An additional point to note is that the interpretation of chance performance, where the RDM comparator equals 0, depends on the chosen RDM comparator, differing, for example, between the Pearson correlation coefficient and the cosine similarity (Diedrichsen et al., 2020).
evidence: Methodological note with supporting citation.

claim: RDM comparators like the Pearson correlation and the cosine similarity are related to the distance correlation, a general indicator of mutual information.
source: RDM comparators like the Pearson correlation and the cosine similarity are related to the distance correlation (Székely et al., 2007), a general indicator of mutual information.
evidence: Relationship between RDM comparators and mutual information with citation.

claim: A significant RDM correlation mainly demonstrates that there is some mutual information between the brain region and the model representation.
source: Like a significant distance correlation, a significant RDM correlation mainly demonstrates that there is some mutual information between the brain region in question and the model representation.
evidence: Interpretation of significant RDM correlations.

claim: For a visual representation, all that is required for a significant RDM correlation is for the two representations to contain some shared information about the input images.
source: For a visual representation, for example, all that is required is for the two representations to contain some shared information about the input images.
evidence: Example of what is required for significant RDM correlation.

claim: Negative RDM correlations can occur, indicating that pairs of stimuli close in one representation tend to be far in the other and vice versa.
source: In contrast to the distance correlation (and other nonnegative estimates of mutual information), however, negative RDM correlations can occur, indicating simply that pairs of stimuli close in one representation tend to be far in the other and vice versa.
evidence: Property of RDM correlations.

claim: Omnibus tests for the presence of information about experimental conditions in a brain region have been introduced in previous studies.
source: Omnibus tests for the presence of information about the experimental conditions in a brain region have been introduced in previous studies (e.g. Kriegeskorte et al., 2006; Allefeld et al., 2016; Nili et al., 2020).
evidence: Reference to previous work on omnibus tests with citations.

claim: Whether stimulus information is present in a region is closely related to whether the noise ceiling is significantly larger than 0, indicating RDM replicability.
source: Whether stimulus information is present in a region is closely related to the question whether the noise ceiling is significantly larger than 0, indicating RDM replicability.
evidence: Relationship between information presence and noise ceiling.

claim: Such tests can sensitively detect small amounts of information in measured activity patterns and can be helpful to assess whether there is any signal for model comparisons.
source: Such tests can sensitively detect small amounts of information in the measured activity patterns and can be helpful to assess whether there is any signal for model comparisons.
evidence: Utility of omnibus tests.

claim: If there is no reliable representational geometry, there is no need to bother with model comparisons.
source: If we are uncertain whether there is a reliable representational geometry to be explained, we need not bother with model comparisons.
evidence: Practical recommendation.

claim: The question whether an individual dissimilarity is significantly larger than zero is equivalent to whether the distinction between two conditions can be decoded from brain activity.
source: The question whether an individual dissimilarity is significantly larger than zero is equivalent to the question whether the distinction between the two conditions can be decoded from the brain activity.
evidence: Relationship between dissimilarity and decoding.

claim: Decoding analyses can be used to test whether individual dissimilarities are significantly larger than zero.
source: Decoding analyses can be used for this purpose (Naselaris et al., 2011; Hebart et al., 2014; Tong and Pratte, 2012; Kriegeskorte and Douglas, 2019b).
evidence: Reference to decoding analyses with citations.

claim: Tests of individual dissimilarities require care because the discriminability of two conditions cannot be systematically negative.
source: Such tests require care because the discriminability of two conditions cannot be systematically negative (Allefeld et al., 2016).
evidence: Methodological caution with supporting citation.

claim: Comparisons between RDMs can be systematically negative, in contrast to discriminability of two conditions.
source: This is in contrast to comparisons between RDMs, which can be systematically negative (although, as mentioned above, they tend to be positive in practice).
evidence: Contrast between RDM comparisons and condition discriminability.

claim: Statistical inference gains power when more data are collected along any dimension.
source: Statistical inference gains power when more data are collected along any dimension. More independent measurement channels, more subjects, more conditions, and more repetitions all help.
evidence: General principle of statistical inference.

claim: How much data is needed along each dimension depends on the experiment.
source: How much data is needed along each of these dimensions depends on the experiment.
evidence: Context-dependent nature of data requirements.

claim: The most helpful dimension to extend is the one that currently limits generalization.
source: The most helpful dimension to extend is the one that currently limits generalization.
evidence: Practical recommendation for experimental design.

claim: When crossvalidation across repeated measurements is used to eliminate bias of distance estimates, using more repetitions brings an additional performance bonus by reducing the variance increase associated with unbiased estimates.
source: When crossvalidation across repeated measurements is used to eliminate the bias of the distance estimates (as in the crossnobis estimator), using more repetitions brings an additional performance bonus because it reduces the variance increase associated with unbiased estimates (Diedrichsen et al., 2020, Appendix 5).
evidence: Benefit of more repetitions with supporting citation.

claim: The statistical inference procedures work for any choice of representational-distance estimator and RDM comparator.
source: The statistical inference procedures introduced here work for any choice of representational-distance estimator and RDM comparator.
evidence: Generality of the methods.

claim: The choice of distance estimator and RDM comparator affects the power of model-comparative inference and the meaning of the inferential results.
source: However, the choice of distance estimator and RDM comparator affects the power of model-comparative inference and the meaning of the inferential results.
evidence: Importance of methodological choices.

claim: Only variations of the crossnobis distance estimator were tested for computing the RDM, as recommended based on earlier research.
source: For computing the RDM, we tested only variations of the crossnobis (crossvalidated Mahalanobis) distance estimator, as recommended based on earlier research (Walther et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of the distance estimator used with supporting citation.

claim: The crossnobis estimator can use different noise covariance estimates to normalize patterns.
source: The crossnobis estimator can use different noise covariance estimates to normalize patterns, such that the noise distribution becomes approximately isotropic. The noise covariance matrix can be the identity (no normalization), diagonal (univariate normalization), or a full estimate (multivariate normalization).
evidence: Description of noise normalization options.

claim: Univariate noise normalization is always preferable to no normalization.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Walther et al., 2016; Ritchie et al., 2021), our results suggest that univariate noise normalization is always preferable to no normalization
evidence: Result from analyses with supporting citations.

claim: Multivariate noise normalization using a shrinkage estimate helps in some circumstances and never hurts model discrimination.
source: and that multivariate noise normalization using a shrinkage estimate of the noise covariance (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004; Schäfer and Strimmer, 2005) helps in some circumstances and never hurts model discrimination.
evidence: Result from analyses with supporting citations.

claim: RDM comparison methods can be distinguished by the scale they assume for the distance estimates: ordinal, interval, or ratio.
source: For evaluating RDM predictions, we can distinguish RDM comparison methods by the scale they assume for the distance estimates: ordinal, interval, or ratio.
evidence: Classification of RDM comparison methods.

claim: For ordinal comparisons, the different rank correlation coefficients perform similarly.
source: For ordinal comparisons, the different rank correlation coefficients perform similarly.
evidence: Result from analyses.

claim: For interval- and ratio-scale comparisons, whether cosine similarities or Pearson correlations work better depends on the structure of the model RDMs to be compared.
source: For interval- and ratio-scale comparisons, a more complex pattern emerges. In particular whether cosine similarities (ratio scale) or Pearson correlations (interval scale) work better depends on the structure of the model RDMs to be compared.
evidence: Result from analyses.

claim: Whitened variants of the cosine similarity and Pearson correlation take into account that the distance estimates in an RDM are not independent.
source: We recently proposed whitened variants of the cosine similarity and Pearson correlation, which take into account that the distance estimates in an RDM are not independent (Diedrichsen et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of whitened RDM comparators with citation.

claim: The whitened RDM comparators were more sensitive to subtle differences in model performance when evaluated on fixed models.
source: The whitened RDM comparators were more sensitive to subtle differences in model performance when evaluated on fixed models (Figure 5c).
evidence: Result from analyses with reference to figure.

claim: In simulations based on calcium-imaging data, whitened RDM comparators performed better on average, but some cortical areas were easier to identify using unwhitened comparison measures.
source: In the simulations based on the calcium-imaging data, whitened RDM comparators still performed better on average, but there were some cortical areas that were easier to identify by using the unwhitened comparison measures.
evidence: Result from calcium-imaging simulations.

claim: A frequentist inference methodology is presented that uses crossvalidation to obtain point estimates of model performance and bootstrapping to estimate uncertainty.
source: We present a frequentist inference methodology that uses crossvalidation to obtain point estimates of model performance and bootstrapping to estimate our uncertainty about them.
evidence: Summary of the methodological approach.

claim: Bayesian alternatives deserve consideration.
source: Bayesian alternatives deserve consideration.
evidence: Acknowledgment of alternative approaches.

claim: A Bayesian approach has been proposed to alleviate the bias of distance estimates.
source: For example, a Bayesian approach has been proposed to alleviate the bias of distance estimates (Cai et al., 2019).
evidence: Reference to alternative approach with citation.

claim: The Bayesian estimate makes more detailed assumptions about trial dependencies than crossvalidated distance estimators.
source: This Bayesian estimate makes more detailed assumptions about the trial dependencies than our crossvalidated distance estimators, which remove the bias.
evidence: Comparison of Bayesian and crossvalidation approaches.

claim: The Bayesian estimate might be preferable for its higher stability when its assumptions hold and could be used in combination with the proposed model-comparative inference methods.
source: The Bayesian estimate might be preferable for its higher stability when its assumptions hold and could be used in combination with our model-comparative inference methods.
evidence: Potential advantage of Bayesian approach.

claim: For model comparisons, Bayesian inference is an interesting alternative to the frequentist methods.
source: For model comparisons, Bayesian inference is also an interesting alternative to the frequentist methods we discuss here (Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen, 2016).
evidence: Reference to Bayesian alternative with citation.

claim: Whitened RDM comparison methods can be motivated as approximations to the likelihood for a model.
source: Our whitened RDM comparison methods can be motivated as approximations to the likelihood for a model
evidence: Theoretical motivation for whitened RDM comparators.

claim: Whitened RDM comparators afford similar power as likelihood-based inference with normal assumptions.
source: and we reported recently that they afford similar power as likelihood-based inference with normal assumptions (Diedrichsen et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison to likelihood-based inference with citation.

claim: Frequentist inference using whitened RDM comparators is related to Bayesian inference with a uniform prior across models.
source: Thus, frequentist inference using the whitened RDM comparators is related to Bayesian inference with a uniform prior across models.
evidence: Relationship between frequentist and Bayesian approaches.

claim: In the Bayesian framework, generalization to the populations of subjects and conditions would require a model of how RDMs vary across subjects and conditions.
source: In the Bayesian framework, generalization to the populations of subjects and conditions would require a model of how RDMs vary across subjects and conditions.
evidence: Requirement for Bayesian generalization.

claim: There is currently no model of how RDMs vary across subjects and conditions.
source: We currently do not have such a model.
evidence: Current limitation of Bayesian approaches.

claim: Until models of RDM variability and Bayesian inference procedures for them are developed, the frequentist methods remain the only method for generalization to the populations of subjects and conditions.
source: Until such models and Bayesian inference procedures for them are developed, the frequentist methods we present here remain the only method for generalization to the populations of subjects and conditions.
evidence: Current advantage of the proposed frequentist methods.

claim: Pattern component modeling is another strongly related method for comparing models to data in terms of their geometry.
source: Another strongly related method for comparing models to data in terms of their geometry is pattern component modeling (Diedrichsen et al., 2018), which compares conditions in terms of their covariance over measurement channels instead of their representational dissimilarities.
evidence: Reference to related method with citation.

claim: Pattern component modeling is deeply related to representational similarity analysis.
source: This approach is deeply related to representational similarity analysis (Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017).
evidence: Relationship between methods with citation.

claim: Pattern component modeling is somewhat more rigid than RSA as the theory is based on normal distributions, but it has advantages in terms of analytical solutions.
source: Pattern component modeling is somewhat more rigid than RSA as the theory is based on normal distributions, but it has advantages in terms of analytical solutions.
evidence: Comparison of pattern component modeling and RSA.

claim: In pattern component modeling, the likelihood of models can be directly evaluated, enabling tests based on the likelihood ratio.
source: In particular, the likelihood of models can be directly evaluated, enabling tests based on the likelihood ratio.
evidence: Advantage of pattern component modeling.

claim: Pattern component modeling can be combined with Bayesian inference more easily, and a variational Bayesian analysis was recently presented for this model.
source: Due to the direct evaluation of likelihoods, this framework can be combined with Bayesian inference more easily and recently a variational Bayesian analysis was presented for this model (Friston et al., 2019).
evidence: Advantage of pattern component modeling with citation.

claim: Another powerful approach to inference on brain-computational models is to fit encoding models that predict measured brain-activity data instead of representational geometries.
source: Another powerful approach to inference on brain-computational models is to fit encoding models that predict measured brain-activity data instead of representational geometries (e.g. Wu et al., 2006; Kay et al., 2008; Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Naselaris et al., 2011; Wandell and Winawer, 2015; Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017; Cadena et al., 2019a).
evidence: Reference to encoding models with citations.

claim: Encoding models were originally developed in the context of low-dimensional models and measurements.
source: This approach was originally developed in the context of low-dimensional models and measurements.
evidence: Historical context of encoding models.

claim: When models and measurements are both high dimensional, even a linear encoding model can be severely under-constrained.
source: When models and measurements are both high dimensional, even a linear encoding model can be severely under-constrained (Cadena et al., 2019b; Kornblith et al., 2019).
evidence: Challenge for encoding models with citations.

claim: An encoding model requires a combination of substantial fitting data and strong priors on the weights.
source: As a result, an encoding model requires a combination of substantial fitting data and strong priors on the weights.
evidence: Requirement for encoding models.

claim: The predictive model being evaluated comprises the encoding model and the priors on its weights, which complicates the interpretation of results.
source: The predictive model that is being evaluated comprises the encoding model and the priors on its weights (Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017), which complicates the interpretation of the results (Cadena et al., 2019b; Kriegeskorte and Douglas, 2019b).
evidence: Challenge for interpreting encoding model results with citations.

claim: Both model performances and fitted weights can be highly uncertain and/or dependent on the details of the assumed encoding model.
source: Both model performances and the fitted weights can then be highly uncertain and/or dependent on the details of the assumed encoding model.
evidence: Limitation of encoding models.

claim: The additional data and assumptions needed to fit complex encoding models motivate consideration of methods that do not require fitting of a high-parametric mapping from model to measured brain activity.
source: The additional data and assumptions needed to fit complex encoding models motivate the consideration of methods as proposed here that do not require fitting of a high-parametric mapping from model to measured brain activity.
evidence: Motivation for the proposed RSA methods.

claim: The generalization challenges tackled for RSA apply equally to encoding models and pattern component modeling.
source: The generalization challenges that we tackle here for RSA apply equally to encoding models and pattern component modeling.
evidence: Generality of the generalization challenges.

claim: Inferences are often meant to generalize to new subjects and/or experimental conditions.
source: Inferences are often meant to generalize to new subjects and/or experimental conditions.
evidence: Common goal in neuroscience research.

claim: Alternative approaches in their current implementations do not yet enable simultaneous generalization to the populations of experimental conditions and subjects.
source: The alternative approaches, in their current implementations, do not yet enable simultaneous generalization to the populations of experimental conditions and subjects.
evidence: Limitation of alternative approaches.

claim: By default, pattern component modeling and its Bayesian variants assume a single geometry and do not take either subject or condition variability into account.
source: By default pattern component modeling and its Bayesian variants assume a single geometry and thus do not take either subject or condition variability into account.
evidence: Limitation of pattern component modeling.

claim: Variability across subjects can be taken into account in a group-level analysis in pattern component modeling, but this approach does not account for uncertainty due to the sample of experimental conditions.
source: Variability across subjects can be taken into account in a group-level analysis (see e.g. Diedrichsen et al., 2018, 2.7.3), but this approach does not account for uncertainty due to the sample of experimental conditions.
evidence: Limitation of group-level analysis in pattern component modeling with citation.

claim: Encoding models usually follow the machine learning approach with training, validation, and test sets.
source: Encoding models usually follow the machine learning approach with training, validation, and test sets (e.g. Naselaris et al., 2011; Cichy et al., 2019; Cichy et al., 2021).
evidence: Description of encoding model approach with citations.

claim: Uncertainty about model evaluations in encoding models is either not estimated at all or estimated in a secondary analysis based on variability across subjects, cells, or conditions.
source: Uncertainty about the model evaluations is either not estimated at all or estimated in a secondary analysis based on the variability across subjects, cells, or conditions.
evidence: Limitation of uncertainty estimation in encoding models.

claim: Because secondary analysis in encoding models is based solely on the test set, results are conditional on the training and validation sets and fall short of generalizing model-comparative inferences to the underlying populations.
source: Because these secondary analysis is based solely on the test set, results are conditional on the training and validation sets, and so fall short of generalizing model-comparative inferences to the underlying populations.
evidence: Limitation of encoding model inference.

claim: The bootstrapping and crossvalidation approaches introduced are not inherently specific to RSA and could be adapted for other model evaluation measures.
source: Note that the bootstrapping and crossvalidation approaches we introduce here are not inherently specific to RSA. These methods could be adapted for estimating the uncertainties about other model evaluation measures such as those provided by pattern component and encoding models.
evidence: Generality of the proposed methods.
